power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p>0.05", "p > 0.05"), Sentence = c("Viable cells were recovered from all groups, with mean viability of 86% in HOPE 20h, 81% in HOPE 4h, and 77% in SCS 4h, and no statistically significant differences between groups (p>0.05) (Fig 5B-E).", "No statistically significant differences were observed between groups (p > 0.05)" )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Background: Hypothermic oxygenated perfusion (HOPE) may extend donor heart preservation beyond conventional storage durations.
We evaluated early graft function and myocardial cellular and metabolic integrity following porcine heart transplantation after 20 hours of HOPE.

Methods: Ten donor hearts underwent various preservation conditions: static cold storage (SCS) for 4 hours (n=2), HOPE for 4 hours (n=3), and HOPE for 20 hours (n=5), followed by heart transplantation (HT) in recipient pigs.

Graft function was monitored over 3 hours by serial echocardiography, invasive hemodynamics, optical flow analysis, and vasoactive support scoring; myocardial tissue was analyzed by histopathology, flow cytometry, mitochondrial respirometry, transcriptomics, and proteomics.
Results: Ejection fraction, right atrial pressure and systolic blood pressure did not differ between groups, and no graft met criteria for primary graft dysfunction.
LV contractility was within normal range with comparable vasoactive support among all groups.
Preservation-associated weight gain was greatest after HOPE 20h, and histopathology showed comparable findings with edema present in all cohorts, without fibrosis, thrombosis, or necrosis.
Cardiomyocyte viability was preserved across all groups.
Maximal oxygen consumption rate was elevated in HOPE 20h versus HOPE 4h and SCS 4h, while basal and non-mitochondrial respiration were similar.
Transcriptomics and proteomics revealed limited differences in gene and pathway expression among groups.

Conclusions: HOPE preserves donor heart viability, mitochondrial integrity, and ventricular function after 20 hours of preservation, without evidence of primary graft dysfunction, supporting extended preservation for heart transplantation.
Edema, recovery of function, and metabolic responses warrant further investigation with longer-term monitoring.

Heart transplantation (HT) provides the greatest clinical improvement and quality-of-life benefit for patients with end-stage heart failure beyond medical therapy and mechanical circulatory support (MCS), yet the supply of suitable donor hearts remains insufficient. [1] [2] [3] [4] Expanded donation criteria have increased the donor pool, but at the cost of more high-risk grafts, a risk that must be weighed against waitlist morbidity and mortality. [5] [6] [7] Geographic reach is also limited by the maximum tolerated ischemic time of roughly 4-6 hours for static cold storage (SCS), the current clinical standard, beyond which early graft dysfunction, rejection, and poor outcomes become more likely. [8] [9] [10] Improved preservation technology could extend this window and enable recovery of high-risk grafts. [11] [12] [13] Hypothermic machine perfusion (HOPE) has emerged as a novel storage strategy that may safely extend the tolerated storage time. 14 HOPE supplies continuous oxygen and nutrient delivery to the heart while maintaining a cold, arrested state using a solution composed of donor blood and cardioplegia perfused through an aortic root cannula.

text.text: Anesthesia, procurement, cardioplegia, and implantation details are in the Supplementary Methods.
After native cardiectomy, donor hearts were implanted using bicaval technique.
Animals were maintained on full CPB for 1 hour after reperfusion, then weaned over 30 minutes, with CPB discontinued at 1.5 hours.

The chest was left open and animals were monitored for 3 hours after separation from CPB, with hemodynamics and vasoactive support recorded every 15 minutes, and arterial blood gases and serum chemistries hourly.
Anesthetic, hemodynamic, arrhythmia, and ventilator management are described in the Supplementary Methods.

The primary outcome was primary graft dysfunction (PGD), defined as: (1) failure to separate from cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) with adequate hemodynamics after a 1.5-hour rest and weaning protocol; (2) LVEF <40% with persistently insufficient hemodynamics despite high-dose inotropes; or (3) right atrial pressure (RAP) >15 mmHg.

text.text: In this study, 20-hour hypothermic oxygenated perfusion supported successful porcine heart transplantation: all hearts were weaned from cardiopulmonary bypass, and none met study-defined criteria for primary graft dysfunction during the three-hour observation period.
Ejection fraction and systemic hemodynamics did not differ between groups, and LV contractility, although lower after HOPE 20h than HOPE 4h at two hours, remained within the normal range.

Extended HOPE showed cell viability comparable to clinical controls and preserved mitochondrial respiratory capacity, with distinct transcriptomic and proteomic changes in inflammatory signaling, RNA processing, and energy metabolism and limited RNA-protein concordance.
It was also accompanied by heart weight gain and interstitial edema.
Edema remains one of the main barriers to clinical translation and a priority for mitigation and longer postoperative monitoring studies.
Retained myocardial cell viability after 20h HOPE complements the observed early graft recovery and extends our previous benchtop findings into in vivo heart transplant model.

The elevated maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) observed in the HOPE 20h group likely reflects a compensatory mitochondrial response to the cumulative stress of prolonged ischemia and reperfusion, rather than a marker of more robust tissue health. 23, 24 In separate work applying this same Seahorse respirometry assay to grossly necrotic, non-viable myocardium, we did not observe this compensatory elevation in OCR or ECAR; rather, energy production in severely injured tissue was uniformly and substantially depressed, with no comparable rise in any parameter (Supplemental Fig. 2).

text.text: This suggests that the elevated maximal OCR seen in HOPE 20h hearts represent still-viable myocardium actively performing oxidative metabolism to compensate for and repair ischemicreperfusion injury, rather than a failing or irreversibly injured tissue bed.

Our data, and others, suggest that hearts preserved with HOPE for up to 20 hours retain sufficient function to undergo transplantation. 20 However, the intermediate and long-term consequences of the observed diastolic dysfunction and impaired lusitropy in the setting of pronounced myocardial edema are unknown.

text.text: Importantly, edema and diastolic dysfunction were also observed in our SCS cohort and are frequently observed in current practice.

Though some amount of edema and diastolic dysfunction are inherent to both heart transplantation, and native to a porcine model, it is highly likely HOPE is a separate contributing factor to interstitial edema. 24, 25 The continuous perfusion of the graft with preservation solution may contribute to the edema and weight gain observed after HOPE preservations.

text.text: Additionally, we observed a reduction in perfusion rate as preservation time elapsed.
Therefore, we hypothesize there is a component of coronary vasoconstriction and/or myocardial stiffness that contributes to increased vascular resistance, resulting in reduced flow.

Mitigating this edemaassociated diastolic impairment by targeting the underlying mechanisms represents an important and clinically actionable next step for future studies aimed at optimizing and extending the HOPE preservation platform.
Several limitations of this study warrant discussion.

The small, unequal cohorts, particularly the SCS 4h group (n=2), compared with HOPE 4h (n=3) and HOPE 20h (n=5), limit statistical power, and nonsignificant differences should not be interpreted as equivalence.
Larger experimental cohorts are needed to strengthen these comparisons.

Additionally, this study did not include long-term survival data; animals were not recovered to an intensive care setting, and the longer-term functional trajectory and recovery potential of hearts preserved for 20 hours with HOPE remains presently unknown.

text.text: Our in vivo large animal model of HT was carried out using female 4 month-old Yorkshire pigs weighing approximately 60-65kg.
All hearts were harvested using a standard, clinically accepted procurement technique with bicaval implantation following donation after brain death (DBD).
Hearts were stored in SCS for 4 hours or HOPE for 4 or 20 hours before implant.
Due to institutional policy, donor pigs were not subject to any procedure to inflict brain death.
The protocol was approved by Columbia's Institute for Comparative Medicine (ICM) under protocol number AC-AACA3703 and all procedures were performed at Columbia University Medical Center.
Prior to transplant procedure, three Yorkshire pigs 60-70kg were sedated and 5mL of blood is withdrawn for blood typing.
Eldon Blood Typing Kit (Eldon Biologicals Home Kit 2511) was used to determine blood type for donor-recipient matching.
All animals were made NPO at least 8 hours prior to surgery.
Both the donor and recipient pig were sedated using 4.5 mg/kg of Telazol and 1.0 mg/kg of Propofol with maintenance by administering 1%-5% inhaled isoflurane.
Pigs were orally intubated and mechanically ventilated with a tidal volume of 10 mL/kg/min, a rate of 10-15 breaths per minute was maintained for the remainder of the procedure.
A water-based veterinary ointment was applied directly to the pig's corneas for lubrication.
IV catheters were placed within the bilateral auricular veins.
Muscle paralysis of the donor was achieved using 0.2 mg/kg of vecuronium.
Fentanyl infusion at 25-100 μg/h given for analgesia.
Monitoring equipment for electrocardiogram monitoring, non-invasive blood pressure, and pulse oximetry were placed.
Mechanical ventilation with a tidal volume of 10 mL/kg/min, a rate of 10-15 breaths per minute was maintained for the remainder of the procedure.
Heart rate (60-100 bpm) and systolic blood pressure (90-130 mmHg) were maintained.
Pigs were positioned supine, scrubbed with a Providine-iodine 8.3% with isopropyl alcohol 72.5% antiseptic solution, and draped for median sternotomy in standard fashion.
Once an appropriate plane of anesthesia was reached, a median sternotomy was performed.
A sternal retractor was placed, the thymus was excised, and a pericardial well was created with traction stitches.
A baseline functional assessment of the donor heart was performed.
Echocardiography, using long and short axis views from the epicardial surface, was used to assess baseline function.
Once preliminary assessment was obtained, the heart was prepared for procurement.
Heparin was administered (350 units/kg).
The right atrium is cannulated with a dual-stage 30-36Fr venous cannula, clamped, and connected to a cell saver.
The proximal ascending aorta is cannulated with a 9 Fr antegrade cardioplegia cannula.
After sufficient cardiac and great vessel dissection, the right atrial cannula was opened.
The left atrial appendage was also opened widely; the ascending aorta was cross-clamped, and cold cardioplegia was delivered.
Cold saline slush was used topically to cool the heart once an arrest was confirmed.
After monitoring for LV distention and adequate root pressure throughout the period of cardioplegia delivery, the heart was excised in standard fashion.
Care was taken to harvest sufficient aortic length to facilitate loading into the XVIVO Heart Assist Transport.

Prior to initiating HOPE, the cardioplegia cannulation site was closed and reinforced, the left atrial appendage was closed with running suture, a 5F sheath was secured within the appendage suture line for placement of the solid-state catheter, and a silastic shunt is placed across the mitral valve and sutured in place to ensure adequate LV venting.
2 liters of histidine-tryptophan-ketoglutarate (HTK) was used for cardioplegic arrest for hearts allocated to the SCS group.
SCS hearts were submerged in HTK solution throughout preservation and stored at 4-6 ˚C. The hearts allocated to the HOPE group were arrested using XVIVO Heart Solution.
XVIVO Heart Solution was also used to prime the perfusion box with 350cc of packed RBCs.

One of the 1000cc priming bags of XVIVO Heart Solution was supplemented with 3ml of XVIVO Heart Solution Supplement, 20 IU Insulin, 50mg imipenem, 5000 IU unfractionated heparin and 10mmol of potassium. 100mEq of sodium bicarbonate is added to preservation box.
HOPE hearts stored for 4 hours were arrested with 1L XHS.
HOPE hearts stored for 20 hours were arrested with 2L XHS.
Preservations were set at standard XVIVO recommendations: aortic root pressure of 20 mmHg and temperature of 8 ˚C.
Recipient pigs were anesthetized and prepped in similar fashion to the donor as described above.
Femoral vein central line insertion and arterial catheterization was performed using ultrasound guidance and Seldinger's technique.
All inotropes and vasopressors were administered centrally.
Urethral catheterization in female swine is challenging due to anatomical conformation.
Suprapubic access provides a reliable and simple alternative for direct bladder cannulation and Foley placement prior to recipient operation 30 .

A catheter is inserted directly to the inferior, dependent portion of the bladder.
The skin was closed and the catheter was secured to the skin.
Median sternotomy was performed in standard fashion, the thymus was removed, and a pericardial well is created.
Heparin was given with confirmation of ACT > 350.

text.text: Aortic and bicaval cannulas for CPB were inserted, and CPB was initiated.
The distal ascending aorta was cross clamped, and recipient cardiectomy was performed in standard fashion.
The left hemi-azygous vein was ligated.
The donor heart was removed from SCS or HOPE preservation and brought onto the field.
Standard bicaval implantation was performed.

Prior to completion of the left atrial anastomosis, a solid-state pressure catheter was inserted through the previously placed sheath in the left atrial appendage into the left atrium and advanced beyond the mitral valve orifice into the left ventricle.
Following completion of the final anastomosis and removal of the aortic cross-clamp, the heart was reperfused while pigs remained on cardiopulmonary bypass.
Defibrillation was required to restore sinus rhythm in most cases, typically necessitating 15-30 minutes of intermittent defibrillation attempts with 10-30J using internal paddles.
During the reperfusion period; spontaneous return of sinus rhythm without defibrillation occurred in one 20-hour HOPE experiment.

Animals were maintained on full cardiopulmonary bypass support for one hour following reperfusion before initiating a slow wean, with flow reduced in a stepwise fashion at approximately 500-1000 mL/min decrements.
Inotropic and vasopressor support was titrated as needed during weaning as described above.

In our initial two experiments, pigs were cooled to 34°C during bypass; in later experiments, active cooling was discontinued to reduce shivering, which seemed to limit lactatemia once bypass was initiated.
Vecuronium was administered for neuromuscular blockade to further suppress shivering once CPB was initiated.
The chest was left open throughout the experiment.
Animals were monitored for a 3-hour terminal observation period.
Vitals were recorded at 15-minute intervals throughout the monitoring period.
Concurrent infusion rates of epinephrine, dobutamine, vasopressin, norepinephrine, amiodarone, and any additional vasoactive infusions were recorded at each time point.
Right atrial pressure, urine output, arterial blood gas, and serum chemistries were assessed at hourly intervals.
Short axis epicardial echocardiography was performed hourly to assess graft function.
Total 'ischemic time' was calculated as the interval between donor aortic cross-clamp application and removal of the recipient aortic cross-clamp.
Anesthetic Maintenance: Animals were maintained on a continuous rate infusion (CRI) of fentanyl and propofol with low-concentration isoflurane 2-5%.
Ketamine CRI was sometimes added, particularly when hemodynamic support was needed while minimizing isoflurane and opioid requirements.
During induced hypothermia on cardiopulmonary bypass, CRI rates was reduced proportionally to account for decreased metabolic demand.
Immunosuppression: Methylprednisolone 1 g by IV was administered as a bolus at the start of the procedure.
If mycophenolate mofetil was indicated per protocol, it was administered via orogastric gavage using a largebore rubber catheter.
Hemodynamic Support: Epinephrine and norepinephrine were prepared in advance as the primary vasopressors.
Initial management of hypotension consisted of reducing isoflurane while increasing propofol CRI and optimizing volume status.
Vasopressors were titrated if hypotension persisted or if myocardial contractility was impaired.

Anticoagulation and Reversal: Heparin was administered immediately prior to cannulation for cardiopulmonary bypass, with activated clotting time (ACT) monitored by the perfusion team targeting 350+ seconds.
Additional heparin boluses were given as needed to maintain therapeutic anticoagulation.
Upon separation from bypass, protamine was dosed based on the total cumulative heparin administered and infused slowly to minimize adverse hemodynamic effects.
Temperature Management: Intentional hypothermia was induced by the perfusion team during bypass, with core body temperature permitted to decrease to approximately 34°C (94°F).
Active warming devices were discontinued upon initiation of bypass and restarted during the rewarming phase prior to separation.
Temperature decline during this period was expected and required no intervention.
In latter experiments, cooling by CPB was terminated, lactate elevation was not observed.
Antiarrhythmic Therapy: Lidocaine IV bolus (1mg/kg) was given for acute arrhythmia management.
Amiodarone was used for antiarrhythmic prophylaxis.
It must be diluted to 2 mg/mL in 5% dextrose in sterile water.
A loading dose of 2 mg/kg is infused over approximately 20 minutes, followed by a maintenance infusion of 1 mg/kg/hr.
Vecuronium was administered when neuromuscular blockade was desired, particularly to suppress shivering during hypothermia.
A CRI of 4-8 mL/hr was typical, with supplemental boluses of 2-6 mL given for breakthrough muscular activity after confirming adequate anesthetic depth.
When the animal is paralyzed and fully supported on bypass, anesthetic depth was confirmed with firm pressure applied between the digits of a forelimb.

Ventilator Management: Mechanical ventilation was maintained throughout the procedure, including during cardiopulmonary bypass, with positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) set at 4 cmH₂O. Tidal volume and respiratory rate was reduced during bypass to minimize barotrauma while preventing atelectasis.
Cardiac graft function was serially assessed using echocardiography, invasive hemodynamic monitoring, and a composite vasoactive support score.

Visual ejection fraction (EF), fractional area change, and left ventricular end diastolic diameter (LVEDD) were measured by echocardiography at donor baseline (prior to cardiectomy) and at 0.5, 1.5, and 2.5 hours following separation from cardiopulmonary bypass by parasternal short axis, via direct epicardial contact.
Left ventricular contractility was assessed via the left ventricular solid-state pressure catheter at 1 and 2 hours off bypass.
Central venous pressure and systolic blood pressure were recorded at 1 and 2 hours following separation from bypass.
A combined drip score, reflecting cumulative vasoactive and inotropic support, was calculated at 1 and 2 hours off bypass by adding epinephrine and levophed dosing.
Statistical comparisons between groups at each timepoint were performed using ANOVA.
Hemodynamics Optical Flow: Quantified Epicardial Motion.
High-definition video of cardiac contraction was obtained at baseline, prior to donor cardiectomy, and after implant throughout the monitoring period (1.5h and 2.5h off CPB).
Once obtained, the videos were stabilized and analyzed using a custom Python pipeline to quantify epicardial motion and estimate contractile function 29 .
text.formatted: Once obtained, the videos were stabilized and analyzed using a custom Python pipeline to quantify epicardial motion and estimate contractile function <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> .

text.text: Videos were converted to grayscale, and frame-frame pixel displacement in a standardized area at interventricular groove that includes both the right ventricle (RV) and the left ventricle (LV) was estimated using the Farnebäck dense optical flow algorithm in OpenCV 30 .
text.formatted: Videos were converted to grayscale, and frame-frame pixel displacement in a standardized area at interventricular groove that includes both the right ventricle (RV) and the left ventricle (LV) was estimated using the Farnebäck dense optical flow algorithm in OpenCV <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> .

text.text: Motion magnitude was averaged and converted from pixels/frame to mm/s using frame rate metadata and a calibration factor in the field of view.
Raw velocity was smoothed through a Savitzy-Golay filter to obtain average velocity magnitudes throughout the cardiac cycle.
To isolate systolic function, velocity values during each ventricular contraction were plotted, and the peak velocities were identified and averaged to obtain mean peak velocity (MPV) of each group.
Furthermore, velocity plots were mathematically differentiated to obtain mean peak acceleration (MPA) of the epicardium during contraction.
Statistical significance was calculated with one-way ANOVA.
At the conclusion of the three-hour post-wean monitoring period, blood and tissue collection was performed immediately.

Hearts were explanted while still warm and beating and immediately processed for downstream analyses, including flow cytometry, histology, mitochondrial respirometry (Seahorse assay) and RNA isolation and sequencing.
The explanted heart was systematically biopsied using a 8mm biopsy punch across left ventricular (LV) free wall and interventricular septum (IVS).
Myocardial tissue obtained from LV and IVS regions was fixed in 10% formalin (4% formaldehyde) for < 24 hours, then transferred to 70% ethanol and embedded in paraffin.
text.formatted: Myocardial tissue obtained from LV and IVS regions was fixed in 10% formalin (4% formaldehyde) for < 24 hours, then transferred to 70% ethanol and embedded in paraffin.

text.text: Next, tissue blocks were sliced using a microtome and 10 µm-tick sections were stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) and Masson's trichrome for histological evaluation.
text.formatted: Next, tissue blocks were sliced using a microtome and 10 µm-tick sections were stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) and Masson's trichrome for histological evaluation.

text.text: Additional 5 µm-tick blank slices were generated for chromogenic terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL) with HRP-DAB system.
Histological specimen preparation and staining were performed in the Molecular Pathology Shared Resource of the Herbert Irving Comprehensive Cancer Center at Columbia University.

Myocardial biopsies of 100 mg were collected from the IVS region, washed immediately in PBS 1x (Corning) and minced into 2 mm 3 using a scalpel blade in sterile conditions under the biosafety cabinet.

Tissues were then transferred into 15 ml tubes containing a warm enzymatic solution consisting of DMEM Base (Gibco, 10313-021) with 450 U/ml Collagenase I (Worthington, LS004196), 60 U/ml DNase I (Millipore, DN25) and 60 U/ml hyaluronidase (Worthington, LS002592) and incubated in a rotating mixer in agitation at 65/70 rpm at 37 °C for 1 hour.

The digestion was stopped by the addition of 8 ml of HBB buffer, consisting of 2% FBS (Sigma-Aldrich, 12306C) and 0.2% BSA (Prometheus, 25-529) in Hanks′ Balanced Salt solution (Gibco, 14175-095), and the single cells suspension was filtered using a 100 µm cell strainer to filter out undigested material and centrifuged at 350g for 5 min at 4 °C. Next, the pellet was resuspended in ACK lysing buffer (Gibco, A10492) to lyse red blood cells, incubated for 5 minutes at room temperature, washed with 9 ml of DMEM Base and centrifuged at 350g for 5 min at 4 °C. After one wash with PBS 1x, cells were incubated for 10 minutes at 4°C in 1 ml of Blocking Solution, consisting of 0.5% BSA in PBS.
Then, 2 ml of PBS 1x were added to the tube and the cellular solution was split equally into three FACS tubes.

Cells were centrifuged at 500g for 5 min at 4°C and the pellet from each FACS tube was resuspended in either 300 µl of Calcein AM (1:500) (BD Pharmingen, 564061) and DRAQ5 (1:2000) (Biolegend, 424101) in PBS, or only DRAQ5 (1:2000) in PBS (Calcein-negative control), or PBS only (unstained control).
Samples were incubated for 30 minutes protected from light at 4°C, then washed with PBS 1x, centrifuged at 500g for 5 min at 4°C and finally resuspended in 300 µl of PBS.
Cells were analyzed using the NovoCyte Penteon Flow Cytometer Systems 5 Lasers (Agilent) and data analysis was performed with the NovoExpress flow cytometry software.
First, single particles were isolated from duplets by plotting Forward Scatter Area (FSC-A) against Forward Scatter Height (FSC-H) and gating only the events that localized along the diagonal line.
Next, nucleated events were identified by DRAQ5 positivity, and, among them, metabolically active cells were identified by Calcein-AM positive staining.
Calcein-AM is a cell-permeant probe that emits a fluorescent signal upon cleavage by cellular esterases and is retained within cells with intact membranes.

Calcein-AM signal is proportional to cell viability and metabolic activity, and it normally decreases in low viable cell samples. 31 Unstained and Calcein-AM negative controls have been used to exclude false positive background signals.
text.formatted: Calcein-AM signal is proportional to cell viability and metabolic activity, and it normally decreases in low viable cell samples. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> Unstained and Calcein-AM negative controls have been used to exclude false positive background signals.

text.text: Precision-Cut Myocardial Slice Preparation: Left ventricular (LV) free wall biopsies were obtained using a full thickness 8 mm punch and washed in 1× PBS.
Biopsy cores were embedded in 3% (w/v) low-gellingtemperature agarose prepared in Tyrode's solution and mounted on a vibrating microtome fitted with a metal blade.
Tissue was sectioned at 150 µm thickness using an advance speed of 1 and oscillation setting of 6 24 , 30 .
text.formatted: Tissue was sectioned at 150 µm thickness using an advance speed of 1 and oscillation setting of 6 24 , <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> .

text.text: Slices were collected and maintained in cardioplegia solution on ice until further processing.

Individual precision-cut slices were further trimmed to 3 mm diameter mini-slices using a biopsy punch, transferred to a wash buffer containing 2% P/S, 5ug/ml gentamycin, 1.25 ug/mL amphotericin B in Advanced DMEM and washed twice for 5 minutes each.
Finally, slices were incubated overnight in Advanced DMEM containing 10% FBS, 1% L-glutamine, 2% P/S, 5 ug/ml gentamycin, 1.25 ug/mL amphotericin B.

Agilent Seahorse XFe96 sensor cartridges were hydrated with 200 µL of tissue-culture-grade deionized water per well and incubated overnight in a non-CO₂ incubator at 37°C. On the day of the assay, hydration water was replaced with 200 µL of XF Calibrant Solution per well.

XF96 cell culture microplates were coated with Corning Cell-Tak tissue adhesive (3.75 µg per well, diluted in deionized water with 0.1 M sodium bicarbonate) for a minimum of 20 minutes to achieve a surface coverage of 5 µg/cm², then washed and allowed to dry prior to slice loading. nIndividual 3 mm × 150 µm myocardial mini-slices were transferred into Cell-Tak-coated wells containing 20 µL PBS to maintain slice flatness.
PBS was removed, and slices were allowed to adhere to the well surface for 1-2 minutes.

Warmed complete Seahorse XF DMEM assay medium (supplemented with 10 mM glucose, 1 mM pyruvate, and 2 mM L-glutamine) was then added to each well to a final volume of 180 µL, taking care to avoid slice detachment. 31 Four wells per plate containing assay medium without tissue served as background.
text.formatted: Warmed complete Seahorse XF DMEM assay medium (supplemented with 10 mM glucose, 1 mM pyruvate, and 2 mM L-glutamine) was then added to each well to a final volume of 180 µL, taking care to avoid slice detachment. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> Four wells per plate containing assay medium without tissue served as background.

text.text: The loaded microplate was incubated for 45-60 minutes in a non-CO₂ incubator at 37°C prior to the assay to allow temperature and pH equilibration.
Mito Stress Test: Mitochondrial function was assessed using a modified Seahorse XF Cell Mito Stress Test (Agilent) on an XFe96/XF Pro Analyzer.
Oligomycin was omitted from the standard protocol, as precision-cut myocardial slices have been reported not to respond reliably to oligomycin dosing 32 , 33 .
text.formatted: Oligomycin was omitted from the standard protocol, as precision-cut myocardial slices have been reported not to respond reliably to oligomycin dosing 32 , <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> .

text.text: Carbonyl cyanide-4 (trifluoromethoxy)phenylhydrazone (FCCP, Port A) and a combination of rotenone and antimycin A (Rot/AA, Port B) were sequentially injected.

FCCP was loaded to a final well concentration of 5 µM and Rot/AA to a final well concentration of 2 µM. 24 The sensor cartridge was calibrated for 15 minutes prior to loading the tissue culture microplate.
text.formatted: FCCP was loaded to a final well concentration of 5 µM and Rot/AA to a final well concentration of 2 µM. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> The sensor cartridge was calibrated for 15 minutes prior to loading the tissue culture microplate.

text.text: Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) were measured over 8 mix-wait-measure cycles (3 minutes mix, 2 minutes wait, 3 minutes measure per cycle) 32 , 24 .
text.formatted: Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) were measured over 8 mix-wait-measure cycles (3 minutes mix, 2 minutes wait, 3 minutes measure per cycle) 32 , <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> .

text.text: Basal OCR and ECAR were recorded prior to FCCP injection; maximal OCR and ECAR were recorded following FCCP-induced uncoupling; and non-mitochondrial OCR was recorded following Rot/AA administration.
OCR and ECAR values were normalized to individual slice volume, calculated from slice diameter (3 mm) and thickness (150 µm).
Raw data were exported and analyzed using Seahorse Analytics software, Microsoft Excel, and GraphPad Prism.
IVS tissue biopsies of approximately 200 mg were homogenized in 1 mL of TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, Cat.
N. 15596026) and stored at -80°C until RNA extraction.
Extraction: RNA extraction and sequencing were performed by GENEWIZ® NGS Services from Azenta Life Sciences (South Plainfield, NJ, USA).
Total RNA was extracted using Qiagen Rneasy Plus Universal Mini kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) following manufacturer's instructions.
RNA samples were quantified using Qubit 4.0 Fluorometer (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and RNA integrity was checked using TapeStation (Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto, CA, USA).
ERCC RNA Spike-In Mix (Cat: #4456740) from ThermoFisher Scientific was added to normalized total RNA prior to library preparation following manufacturer's protocol.

RNA sequencing libraries were prepared using the NEBNext Ultra II RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina and NEBNext Poly(A) mRNA Magnetic Isolation Module (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA, USA), according to manufacturer's recommendations.
Briefly, mRNAs were initially enriched with Oligod(T) beads.

Enriched mRNAs were fragmented for 15 minutes at 94 °C. First strand and second strand cDNA were subsequently synthesized. cDNA fragments were end-repaired and adenylated at 3'ends, and universal adapters were ligated to cDNA fragments, followed by index addition and library enrichment by PCR with limited cycles.
The sequencing library was validated on the Agilent TapeStation, and quantified by using Qubit 4.0 Fluorometer as well as by quantitative PCR (KAPA Biosystems, Wilmington, MA, USA).
The sequencing libraries were multiplexed and clustered onto a flowcell.
After clustering, the flowcell was loaded on the Illumina NovaSeq instrument according to manufacturer's instructions.
The samples were sequenced using a 2x150bp Paired End (PE) configuration.
Image analysis and base calling were conducted by the NovaSeq Control Software.
Raw sequence data (.bcl files) generated from Illumina NovaSeq was converted into fastq files and de-multiplexed using Illumina bcl2fastq 2.20 software.
One mismatch was allowed for index sequence identification.

Differential gene expression analysis was performed using PyDESeq2, a Python implementation of the DESeq2 statistical framework. 34 Raw counts were normalized using the median-of-ratios method to account for differences in sequencing depth and RNA composition.
text.formatted: Differential gene expression analysis was performed using PyDESeq2, a Python implementation of the DESeq2 statistical framework. <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34</ref> Raw counts were normalized using the median-of-ratios method to account for differences in sequencing depth and RNA composition.

text.text: Differential expression was modeled using negative binomial generalized linear models with gene-specific dispersion estimation.
Preservation condition was included as the explanatory variable, with pooled clinical controls serving as the reference group.
Differential expression was evaluated using Wald tests of the null hypothesis that the log₂ fold change between preservation conditions was zero.
Cook's distance-based outlier handling and model refitting were enabled where supported by the available biological replicates.
Resulting P values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate (FDR).

Genes with FDR <0.05 were considered statistically significant, with an additional absolute log₂ fold-change threshold >1 applied to identify differentially expressed genes exhibiting changes greater than twofold.
text.formatted: Genes with FDR <0.05 were considered statistically significant, with an additional absolute log₂ fold-change threshold >1 applied to identify differentially expressed genes exhibiting changes greater than twofold.

text.text: Positive log₂ fold changes indicated increased expression in HOPE20h relative to clinical controls.

Preranked gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed using GSEApy to identify coordinated transcriptional differences in predefined biological pathways. 35 Genes were ranked according to their signed Wald test statistics obtained from PyDESeq2, thereby incorporating both the direction and statistical strength of differential expression.
text.formatted: Preranked gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed using GSEApy to identify coordinated transcriptional differences in predefined biological pathways. <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> Genes were ranked according to their signed Wald test statistics obtained from PyDESeq2, thereby incorporating both the direction and statistical strength of differential expression.

text.text: All eligible genes with finite ranking statistics were included, irrespective of individual gene-level statistical significance or fold-change magnitude.
Enrichment analyses were performed using MSigDB Hallmark 2020 and Gene Ontology Biological Process 2023 gene set collections.
GSEA was performed using 1,000 permutations, a minimum gene set size of 10, a maximum gene set size of 500, and a fixed random seed of 42.
Enrichment scores were calculated according to the distribution of pathway-associated genes within the ranked dataset and normalized to generate normalized enrichment scores (NES).
Statistical significance was assessed using permutation-derived nominal P values and FDR-adjusted q-values, with FDR <0.05 defining significant pathway enrichment.
text.formatted: Statistical significance was assessed using permutation-derived nominal P values and FDR-adjusted q-values, with FDR <0.05 defining significant pathway enrichment.

text.text: Positive NES values indicated relative enrichment in HOPE20h, whereas negative NES values indicated relative enrichment in pooled clinical preservation controls.
Pathway enrichment was interpreted as evidence of coordinated transcriptional differences rather than direct functional activation or inhibition of the corresponding biological processes.

To investigate preservation-associated alterations in cardiac cell-type transcriptional signatures, bulk RNA sequencing data from porcine myocardial samples subjected to static cold storage for 4 hours (SCS4h; n=2), hypothermic oxygenated perfusion for 4 hours (HOPE4h; n=2), or extended hypothermic oxygenated perfusion for 20 hours (HOPE20h; n=4) were analyzed using a custom Python-based pipeline.
Raw gene-level counts were normalized using the median-of-ratios method, with size factors calculated from genes exhibiting nonzero counts across all samples.
Normalized expression values were subsequently log₂-transformed following the addition of a pseudocount of one.

To characterize cell-type-associated transcriptional activity, curated marker gene panels were assembled for cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, macrophages/monocytes, T lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, pericytes, and vascular smooth muscle cells (Supplemental Figure 10A). [36] [37] [38] [39] Candidate marker genes were mapped to porcine Ensemble gene identifiers using MyGene.info (Sus scrofa, NCBI taxonomy ID: 9823).

text.text: Only exact gene-symbol matches with unambiguous gene-level assignments were retained.
Marker coverage was assessed for each cell population, and signatures containing fewer than three successfully mapped, variable genes were excluded.

To evaluate relative cell-type-associated transcriptional activity, log₂-transformed expression values were standardized independently for each gene across all eight biological samples using z-score normalization.

For each sample, cell-type-associated transcriptional signature scores were calculated as the arithmetic mean of the standardized expression values of all successfully mapped marker genes within the corresponding cell-type panel.
Importantly, differences in signature scores cannot distinguish altered cellular abundance from transcriptional regulation within existing cell populations.
The limited number of biological replicates constrained the resolution and statistical power of exact permutation testing, particularly in comparisons involving two control samples.
Raw diaPASEF files were searched against the UniProt Pig proteome database (UP000008227) using DIA-NN (v2.6.0) with default settings for library-free analysis 39 .
text.formatted: Raw diaPASEF files were searched against the UniProt Pig proteome database (UP000008227) using DIA-NN (v2.6.0) with default settings for library-free analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39</ref> .

text.text: Search was performed with trypsin specificity, allowing up to one missed cleavage.

Carbamidomethylation of cysteine (+57.021 Da) was set as a fixed modification, while protein N-terminal acetylation (+42.010 Da), methionine oxidation (+15.995 Da), and deamidation of N/Q (+0.984 Da) were included as variable modifications.
The false discovery rate (FDR) was controlled at 1% at both precursor and protein levels.
DIA-NN output files were further analyzed for differential abundance using DIA-Analyst platform (v0.11.1), without additional normalization.
Missing values were imputed using the Perseus-type imputation method, and FDR was corrected with t-statistics based method.
Proteins with adjusted p-value < 0.05 and absolute log2 fold change >1 were considered differentially abundant between groups.
text.formatted: Proteins with adjusted p-value < 0.05 and absolute log2 fold change >1 were considered differentially abundant between groups.

text.text: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed on quantitative proteomic data to identify biological pathways associated with extended hypothermic oxygenated heart preservation (HOPE20h) relative to pooled clinical preservation controls (SCS4h and HOPE4h).

Preranked GSEA was conducted using GSEApy, with proteins ranked according to a signed statistical significance metric incorporating both the magnitude and direction of differential protein abundance. 44 For each protein, the ranking statistic was calculated as: Ranking statistic = sign(log₂FC) × [-log₁₀(P value)], where log₂FC represented the relative protein abundance in HOPE20h compared with pooled clinical controls, and P represented the nominal P value obtained from differential protein abundance analysis.
text.formatted: Preranked GSEA was conducted using GSEApy, with proteins ranked according to a signed statistical significance metric incorporating both the magnitude and direction of differential protein abundance. <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44</ref> For each protein, the ranking statistic was calculated as: Ranking statistic = sign(log₂FC) × [-log₁₀(P value)], where log₂FC represented the relative protein abundance in HOPE20h compared with pooled clinical controls, and P represented the nominal P value obtained from differential protein abundance analysis.

text.text: When nominal P values were unavailable, log₂ fold changes were used as the alternative ranking metric.
Proteins with nonfinite ranking statistics were excluded, and duplicate gene symbols were removed to retain a single entry per gene.
Preranked enrichment analysis was performed using MSigDB Hallmark 2020, Reactome 2022, and Gene Ontology Biological Process 2023 gene set collections.
Gene sets were evaluated using 1,000 permutations, a minimum gene set size of 5, a maximum gene set size of 500, and a fixed random seed of 42.
All eligible quantified proteins were included in the ranked dataset irrespective of their individual statistical significance.
Enrichment scores were calculated based on the distribution of pathway-associated proteins within the ranked dataset and normalized to generate normalized enrichment scores (NES).
Statistical significance was assessed using permutation-derived nominal P values and false discovery rate (FDR)-adjusted q-values.
Pathways with FDR <0.05 were considered significantly enriched.
text.formatted: Pathways with FDR <0.05 were considered significantly enriched.

text.text: Positive NES values indicated relative enrichment of pathway-associated proteins in HOPE20h, whereas negative NES values indicated relative enrichment in pooled clinical controls.
RNA-protein directional concordance was evaluated using matched gene-protein pairs.

A descriptive absolute log₂ fold-change threshold of 0.25 was applied independently to RNA and protein measurements. 45 Pairs exceeding this threshold in both omics layers were classified as concordantly increased, concordantly decreased, RNA-increased/protein-decreased, or RNA-decreased/protein-increased according to their respective fold-change directions.

text.text: Pairs failing to exceed the threshold in either layer were classified as below the directional threshold.
Directional classifications were descriptive and independent of statistical significance, which was assessed separately using an FDR threshold of <0.05.

Leading-edge analysis was performed using a custom Python pipeline to identify genes contributing to pathway enrichment and characterize redundancy among enriched biological pathways.
Leading-edge gene annotations, normalized enrichment scores (NES), and false discovery rate (FDR) q-values were obtained from the preceding gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA).
Leading-edge genes were extracted from the GSEA results as the subset of pathway-associated genes contributing to the enrichment score at its maximum deviation from zero.
These genes represent the principal contributors to the observed enrichment signal within each pathway.

To assess redundancy among enriched biological pathways, pairwise overlap of leading-edge gene sets was quantified using the Jaccard similarity coefficient defined as the number of shared leading-edge genes divided by the total number of unique genes represented across both pathways.
Gene-pathway relationships were additionally represented using binary membership matrices, indicating whether individual genes belonged to the leading-edge subset of each pathway.
Membership heatmaps included up to 30 genes ranked by their frequency of occurrence across the top 25 significantly enriched pathways by minimum FDR.
These matrices represented pathway membership rather than gene-expression magnitude.
FDR in this analysis is pathway-level GSEA FDR, not gene-level DESeq2 FDR.
A gene appearing in many leading edges is a recurring contributor to pathway enrichment, not automatically a significant DEG or a causal regulator.
The Jaccard threshold (≥ 0.25) and gene-prioritization metrics were considered exploratory analytical criteria rather than independently validated statistical significance thresholds.
Tissue biopsied from the IVS weighting approximately 200 mg was placed in cryotubes, snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80°C until use.
Samples were pulverized and suspended in lysis buffer containing 1% SDC, 2% SDS, and 1× protease inhibitor in 100 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), followed by homogenization using PreOmics' BeatBox for 10 min.
The tubes were then placed on a magnetic rack, and the solubilized lysate was transferred to 1.5 mL Eppendorf tubes.
The lysates were centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 5 min, and the supernatants were transferred to fresh 1.5 mL Eppendorf tubes.
The samples were incubated at 60 °C for 20 min with constant agitation at 1,400 rpm, followed by incubation at room temperature for 5 min and water-bath sonication for 2 min.
Protein concentrations were determined using the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit.
A total of 10 µg of protein from each lysate was used for subsequent processing.
Proteins were reduced and alkylated using 10 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP) and 40 mM 2-chloroacetamide at 45 °C for 10 min with constant agitation at 1,400 rpm.
Following reduction and alkylation, the samples were incubated at room temperature for 5 min and sonicated in a water bath for 2 min.

Lysate cleanup was performed using SP3 magnetic beads, followed by overnight digestion at 37 °C with Lys-C/Trypsin (Promega) at an enzyme-toprotein ratio of 1:100. 37 Digestion was terminated by adding TFA to a final concentration of 1% (v/v).

text.text: The resulting peptide mixtures were clarified by centrifugation at 14,000g for 10 min and desalted using a C18 plate. 41 The eluted peptides were dried using a SpeedVac centrifuge and resuspended in 3% acetonitrile / 0.1% formic acid.
text.formatted: The resulting peptide mixtures were clarified by centrifugation at 14,000g for 10 min and desalted using a C18 plate. <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> The eluted peptides were dried using a SpeedVac centrifuge and resuspended in 3% acetonitrile / 0.1% formic acid.

text.text: An aliquot corresponding to 200 ng of peptides from each sample was subjected to LC-MS/MS analysis.
